title: Supreme Court Lets Trump Resume Border Wall Construction in Big Bend
excerpt: An unsigned 8-1 ruling paused a district judge's injunction against barriers in the Big Bend sector of Texas, holding that Congress's preference for fast border construction outweighs the environmental harm challengers allege.
body:
• The US Supreme Court on Monday lifted a federal judge's order that had halted border wall construction in the Big Bend region of West Texas, including Big Bend National Park.
  • In an unsigned opinion, the court said Congress has shown a "clear preference for expeditious border construction" that outweighs the aesthetic, recreational and environmental harm alleged by challengers.
  • Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only justice to publicly dissent; the ruling lets construction resume while the lawsuit continues in the lower court.
  • The challengers — an environmental group, a local river guide and a group preserving a historic church — argue the administration waived environmental laws without clear authority from Congress.

The US Supreme Court gave the Trump administration the green light on Monday to proceed with construction of barriers along the US-Mexico border in a remote region of West Texas that includes Big Bend National Park, fast-tracking one of the president's longstanding priorities, Reuters reported.

The court granted the administration's emergency request to lift an order by US District Judge Kathleen Cardone in El Paso, who blocked the project in October while a lawsuit against it plays out. The decision pauses that injunction — it does not end the case, which continues in the lower court even as construction resumes.

What the court said

In an unsigned opinion, the court said Congress has expressed a "clear preference for expeditious border construction," which outweighs "any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm" the challengers say they will suffer. The administration, the court found, is likely to succeed in its argument that the district judge lacked the power to block the work. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, one of the court's three liberal justices, was the only justice to publicly dissent, and she did not explain her reasoning. The Wall Street Journal reported the ruling as 8-1.

"The Government's interest therefore outweighs any aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harm alleged by respondents."

— US Supreme Court, unsigned opinion

What is being built, and where

The Big Bend sector spans more than 500 miles of the southern border — more than a quarter of its entire length. The administration says most construction in the sector, covering more than 300 miles of barriers and roads, will take place on privately owned land. Big Bend National Park, about 250 miles southeast of El Paso, would get a 17-mile noncontiguous vehicle barrier system, not the 30-foot pedestrian barriers planned elsewhere, according to the administration. Congress funded the broader border project with $46 billion last summer, the Associated Press reported, and Customs and Border Protection has been erecting barriers at a pace of about 12 miles a week across the border.

The other side of the case

The lawsuit was brought by the Center for Biological Diversity, a Big Bend-area river guide and a group seeking to preserve a historic church in Ruidosa, Texas, whose fragile adobe structure they say is threatened by construction. They challenged waivers issued by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and his predecessor Kristi Noem between February and July, which set aside a range of environmental and conservation laws — among them the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act — to speed the work.

The waivers rest on a 1996 law allowing barriers in areas of "high illegal entry." Judge Cardone found that designation hard to sustain in Big Bend, which has by far the lowest rate of migrant apprehensions of any border sector: if Big Bend qualified, she wrote, every sector would. The administration paused construction in Big Bend in August after bipartisan criticism of the project's impact on the park's landscape and wildlife, then resumed work — including a 47-mile stretch in Hudspeth County begun in September — before Cardone's injunction stopped it again.

What happens next

Construction can now restart while the challengers' lawsuit proceeds. The underlying legal question — whether the waiver authority Congress granted in 1996 is broad enough to cover a project of this scale — remains open, and the case could return to the Supreme Court on the merits. For now, the practical effect is immediate: crews in one of the most remote and ecologically sensitive stretches of the border can go back to work.
